landmarks.name: Paro Taktsang (Tiger's Nest Monastery)
landmarks.writeup: A sacred Himalayan Buddhist site perched on a cliffside, known for its stunning views and spiritual significance.

wiki.extract: Paro Taktsang is a sacred Vajrayana Himalayan Buddhist site located in the cliffside of the upper Paro valley in Bhutan. It is one of thirteen Tiger's Nest caves in historical Tibet in which Padmasambhava practiced and taught Vajrayana.

landmarks.name: Punakha Dzong
landmarks.writeup: An impressive fortress and monastery located at the confluence of two rivers, serving as an important religious and administrative center.

wiki.extract: The Punakha Dzong, also known as Pungthang Dewa Chhenbi Phodrang, is the administrative centre of Punakha District in Punakha, Bhutan. Constructed by Ngawang Namgyal, 1st Zhabdrung Rinpoche, in 1637–38, it is the second oldest and second-largest dzong in Bhutan and one of its most majestic structures. The dzong houses the sacred relics of the southern Drukpa Lineage of the Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism, including the Rangjung Kharsapani and the sacred remains of Ngawang Namgyal and the tertön Pema Lingpa.

landmarks.name: Bumthang Valley
landmarks.writeup: A culturally rich valley known as the spiritual heartland of Bhutan, featuring ancient temples and monasteries.

wiki.extract: Bumthang Valley is the main inhabited valley in the Bumthang district of Bhutan.

cultural_events.name: Tshechu Festivals
cultural_events.writeup: Annual religious festivals held in various districts featuring masked dances, rituals, and community gatherings.

wiki.extract: A tshechu is any of the annual religious Bhutanese festivals held in each district or dzongkhag of Bhutan on the tenth day of a month of the lunar Tibetan calendar. The month depends on the place. Tshechus are religious festivals of the Drukpa Lineage of the Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism.

cultural_events.name: Losar
cultural_events.writeup: Bhutanese New Year celebrated with traditional music, dance, and feasts.

wiki.extract: Losar, also known as the Tibetan New Year, is a festival in Tibetan Buddhism. The holiday is celebrated on various dates depending on location tradition. The holiday is a new year's festival, celebrated on the first day of the lunisolar Tibetan calendar, which corresponds to a date in February or March in the Gregorian calendar. In 2025, the new year commenced on February 28 and was celebrated until March 2. It also commenced the Year of the Female Wood Snake.

food_writeup: Bhutanese cuisine is characterized by its use of chili peppers and cheese, with dishes like Ema Datshi (chili and cheese stew) being a national favorite.
brief_history: Bhutan has maintained its sovereignty and cultural identity through a history of isolation and monarchy, transitioning to a constitutional monarchy in 2008.

commentary.inflation_management: The ngultrum is pegged at par to the Indian rupee, so Bhutan imports India's monetary stance and much of its inflation pattern: inflation ran 8-10% in 2011-14 (peaking at 10.1% in 2012), fell to 2.8-3.6% in 2016-20, then rose to 8.2% in 2021 on the global commodity shock before easing to a projected 2.6% in 2025. Domestic policy has little independent leverage; the Royal Monetary Authority manages liquidity and the peg. The arrangement has delivered reasonable price stability at the cost of vulnerability to Indian inflation cycles and rupee liquidity squeezes.
commentary.debt_management: Bhutan's public debt looks alarming at 103.6% of GDP in the 2025 projection (peaking at 124.5% in 2021, up from 80.1% in 2006), but its composition makes it unusual: the bulk is hydropower project debt owed to India, self-financing through long-term power purchase agreements. The IMF and World Bank have consistently assessed it as sustainable for this reason. Ratios rose as big projects (Punatsangchhu) were built and GDP growth was modest; as plants commission and revenues flow, the ratio is projected to keep declining. The risk is project delays and cost overruns, which have already materialized.

key_events.event: Global crisis slowed growth briefly; hydropower construction continued.
Rupee shortage crisis forced import curbs and a credit squeeze, exposing peg vulnerabilities.
Hydropower investment boom pushed debt toward 90% of GDP.
COVID-19 shut tourism, a key foreign-exchange earner; debt peaked above 115% of GDP.
Hydropower revenues and Indian demand supported recovery; debt began declining.
Debt projected at 103.6% of GDP, still high but on a declining path as projects come online.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: Bhutan's outlook is tied to hydropower commissioning and Indian electricity demand: successful projects bring the debt ratio down steadily and fund development. Tourism recovery and diversification into services offer upside. Risks are concentrated: cost overruns on mega-dams, climate impacts on river flows, and any rupee-liquidity stress under the peg. With debt self-liquidating in principle, the analytical risk is execution, not solvency.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
